public_rationale: This is a claim about what prediction success logically establishes. The proposed empirical test would require an added definition of understanding. Repeated mistakes do not by themselves prove its absence, just as successful predictions do not settle its presence. A binary verdict would depend on the evaluator's philosophical or operational definition.
limitations: This does not reject Marcus's argument or endorse Hinton's.
A narrower claim about a specified prediction measure and comprehension test could be assessed empirically.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Good next-word prediction by LLMs does not necessarily imply understanding.

statement.excerpt: To be fair, large language models aren’t just looking things up, but the idea that a good prediction of next word necessarily implies understanding is fallacious.
statement.document_title: What was 60 Minutes thinking, in that interview with Geoff Hinton?

a good prediction of next word
our_interpretation: Marcus disputes a necessary implication between prediction performance and understanding. He does not claim here that every LLM lacks every form of understanding.

An ordinary reader can distinguish prediction success from comprehension, but the statement supplies neither a prediction threshold nor a sufficiently determinate meaning of understanding for a binary empirical verdict.
Equating understanding with flawless performance on a selected benchmark would add a decisive premise Marcus did not supply. Intelligent humans can also make comprehension errors.
criteria.support_condition: Under specified definitions, demonstrate adequate next-word prediction together with independently established absence of the relevant understanding, or establish a valid counterexample to the proposed implication.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Under those same definitions, establish that the specified prediction performance requires the specified understanding. Examples of models that exhibit both are insufficient.
